task_3.title: Honor testpaths config when loading root conftest files
task_3.description: Fixed a regression where the testpaths configuration option was not considered when loading initial conftest files. When users configured custom test directories via testpaths in their pytest INI config (e.g., a directory other than the default tests/), conftest.py files in those directories were not loaded during startup. This caused hooks defined in those conftest files (such as pytest_sessionstart) to silently not execute. The fix ensures that testpaths entries from the INI configuration are included in the set of paths scanned for root-level conftest loading.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that when testpaths is configured in the pytest INI configuration (e.g., pyproject.toml, pytest.ini, or setup.cfg), conftest.py files located at the root of those configured test directories are loaded during initial conftest discovery. Previously, only explicitly provided command-line paths were used to discover initial conftest files, causing conftest.py hooks (e.g., pytest_sessionstart) in custom test directories to be silently skipped.

expectation.grounded: PytestPluginManager._set_initial_conftests must accept testpaths from the INI configuration (via Config.getini('testpaths')) in addition to the CLI-provided file_or_dir arguments. Both sources of paths must be used when scanning for root-level conftest files. When a conftest.py exists in a directory listed in testpaths, its hooks (e.g., pytest_sessionstart, pytest_sessionfinish) must be invoked during the session lifecycle. This applies regardless of the operating system or the name of the test directory.
expectation.conceptual: When a user configures custom test directories via the testpaths setting, any conftest.py files at the root of those directories must be automatically discovered and loaded. All pytest hooks defined in those conftest files must execute as part of the normal session lifecycle, just as they would if the test directory were the default tests/ directory or explicitly passed on the command line.

constraints.grounded: Conftest loading for CLI-provided paths (namespace.file_or_dir) must not be disrupted. If testpaths is empty or not set, the behavior must be identical to prior versions. If both CLI paths and testpaths are provided, conftest files from both sets of paths must be discovered. The --noconftest flag must still suppress all conftest loading. The --pyargs mode must continue to function correctly.
constraints.conceptual: Existing conftest discovery behavior for explicitly specified paths must remain unchanged. The fix must be additive: it expands the set of paths considered for conftest discovery without altering how previously supported paths are handled. Users who do not use the testpaths configuration option must experience no behavioral difference.

behavior: When testpaths is configured in the pytest INI config, conftest.py files in those directories are now loaded during initial conftest discovery.
Hooks defined in conftest.py files within testpaths directories (e.g., pytest_sessionstart, pytest_sessionfinish, fixtures) are now invoked during the session lifecycle.
The initial conftest scanning now considers the union of CLI-provided paths and testpaths INI entries.
When no testpaths is configured, behavior remains identical to the previous version.
The fix resolves a platform-independent regression that was particularly noticeable on Windows.
acceptance_criteria: Given a pytest INI configuration with testpaths set to a custom directory (e.g., 'some_path'), and a conftest.py in that directory defining pytest_sessionstart, when pytest is invoked without explicit path arguments, then the pytest_sessionstart hook should execute.

Given a pytest INI configuration with testpaths set to a custom directory, and a conftest.py in that directory defining fixtures, when tests in that directory use those fixtures, then the fixtures should be available and resolved correctly.

Given a pytest invocation with both CLI path arguments and testpaths configured, when pytest loads initial conftests, then conftest.py files from both CLI paths and testpaths directories should be loaded.
Given a pytest INI configuration with an empty testpaths value, when pytest is invoked, then conftest loading should behave identically to the prior version.
Given a pytest invocation with the --noconftest flag, when testpaths is configured, then no conftest files should be loaded from any source.

Given a project with testpaths pointing to a non-default directory name on any operating system, when pytest runs, then conftest.py in that directory should be loaded and all hooks therein should execute.

task_4.title: Allow TypedDict arguments in monkeypatch setitem/delitem type annotations
task_4.description: The monkeypatch.setitem and monkeypatch.delitem methods previously annotated their dictionary parameter as MutableMapping, which caused static type checkers like mypy to reject TypedDict arguments even though they worked fine at runtime. The type annotations have been broadened from MutableMapping to Mapping so that TypedDict-typed dictionaries are accepted without type errors. Runtime behavior is unchanged; only the static typing surface is affected.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that monkeypatch.setitem and monkeypatch.delitem accept TypedDict-typed dictionaries without producing static type-checking errors. Previously, passing a TypedDict to these methods caused mypy to report an arg-type error because TypedDict is not compatible with MutableMapping, even though the call succeeded at runtime.

expectation.grounded: The MonkeyPatch.setitem and MonkeyPatch.delitem methods should accept a dictionary parameter typed as Mapping[K, V] instead of MutableMapping[K, V]. This allows TypedDict instances to be passed as the first argument without triggering mypy arg-type errors. The internal _setitem undo stack should also use the Mapping type in its annotation. Running mypy on code that calls monkeypatch.setitem or monkeypatch.delitem with a TypedDict argument should produce no type errors.
expectation.conceptual: The monkeypatch setitem and delitem APIs should accept any dict-like object, including TypedDict instances, without producing static type-checking errors. Users who rely on TypedDict for structured dictionary types should be able to use monkeypatch with those types seamlessly under mypy or similar type checkers.

constraints.grounded: The runtime behavior of MonkeyPatch.setitem, MonkeyPatch.delitem, and the undo logic in MonkeyPatch.undo must remain unchanged. The methods must still perform item assignment, deletion, and restoration on the passed dictionary at runtime. Existing code passing MutableMapping or plain dict arguments must continue to work without any type errors. The broadened Mapping annotation must not introduce new mypy errors on the mutation operations within the method bodies.
constraints.conceptual: Existing tests and user code using monkeypatch with regular dicts or MutableMapping-typed objects must not be affected. The change must be purely at the type-annotation level with no alteration to runtime behavior. The undo/restore mechanism must continue to function correctly for all accepted dictionary types.

behavior: The dic parameter type annotation on MonkeyPatch.setitem changes from MutableMapping[K, V] to Mapping[K, V].
The dic parameter type annotation on MonkeyPatch.delitem changes from MutableMapping[K, V] to Mapping[K, V].
The internal _setitem undo stack type annotation changes from List[Tuple[MutableMapping[Any, Any], object, object]] to List[Tuple[Mapping[Any, Any], object, object]].
Static type checkers (mypy) no longer report arg-type errors when a TypedDict instance is passed to monkeypatch.setitem or monkeypatch.delitem.
Runtime behavior of setitem, delitem, and undo is completely unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: When a TypedDict-typed variable is passed to monkeypatch.setitem, mypy reports no arg-type errors.
When a TypedDict-typed variable is passed to monkeypatch.delitem, mypy reports no arg-type errors.
When a plain dict is passed to monkeypatch.setitem or monkeypatch.delitem, mypy continues to report no type errors.
When a MutableMapping-typed variable is passed to monkeypatch.setitem or monkeypatch.delitem, mypy continues to report no type errors.
When monkeypatch.setitem is called with a TypedDict at runtime, the item is set correctly and undo restores the original value.
When monkeypatch.delitem is called with a TypedDict at runtime, the item is deleted correctly and undo restores the original value.
The MonkeyPatch.setitem method signature uses Mapping as the type for its dictionary parameter.
The MonkeyPatch.delitem method signature uses Mapping as the type for its dictionary parameter.

task_1.title: Fix OSError crash when CLI option values exceed OS filename length limit
task_1.description: When pytest receives a command-line argument with a very long value, it attempts to check whether that argument could be a file or directory path by calling exists() on the resolved path. On systems with filename length limits (e.g., 255 bytes on Linux ext4), this call raises an OSError with errno 36 (File name too long), causing pytest to crash during initial configuration before any test collection occurs. The fix gracefully catches the OSError during the path existence check and treats the unresolvable path as non-existent, allowing pytest to continue normal argument processing.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that pytest does not crash with an OSError when a user passes a command-line option whose value is long enough to exceed the operating system's maximum filename length. Previously, pytest would raise 'OSError: [Errno 36] File name too long' during initial conftest loading when it attempted to check whether such a long argument was a valid file path. This crash prevented pytest from running at all, even though the long value was a legitimate custom option and not intended to be a file path.

expectation.grounded: When PytestPluginManager._set_initial_conftests iterates over file_or_dir arguments and calls exists() on the resolved anchor path, any OSError raised (e.g., due to filename length limits) should be caught and the anchor should be treated as non-existent. The method should continue processing remaining arguments and proceed to normal test session startup without raising an unhandled exception.
expectation.conceptual: When a user invokes pytest with custom command-line options containing very long string values, pytest should gracefully handle the case where those values cannot be resolved as filesystem paths. Instead of crashing, pytest should skip the invalid path and continue with normal test discovery and execution.

constraints.grounded: The OSError handling must only apply to the anchor.exists() call within the initial conftest discovery path. Valid file paths that do exist must still be correctly resolved and their conftests loaded. The fix must not suppress OSError exceptions from other operations (e.g., actual file I/O failures during conftest importing). When anchor.exists() raises OSError, the behavior must be equivalent to the path not existing (i.e., no conftest loading attempted for that anchor).
constraints.conceptual: The fix must not interfere with normal file and directory path resolution. Legitimate test paths and conftest files must continue to be discovered and loaded correctly. Only the specific scenario where a path string triggers an OS-level error during existence checking should be handled gracefully.

behavior: When a CLI argument resolves to a path that exceeds the OS filename length limit, pytest no longer raises an unhandled OSError during startup.
An argument that triggers an OSError on exists() is treated as a non-existent path, meaning no conftest loading is attempted for that argument.
Normal file and directory arguments that are within OS filename limits continue to be checked and processed as before.
The conftest discovery loop continues processing subsequent arguments after encountering one that causes an OSError.
If no valid file anchors are found among the arguments, pytest falls back to its standard behavior for when no anchor paths are discovered.
acceptance_criteria: When a user runs pytest with a custom option value long enough to exceed the OS maximum filename length (e.g., >255 characters on Linux), pytest should start a normal test session instead of crashing with OSError.
When a user runs pytest with a valid file or directory path argument, conftest files should still be discovered and loaded correctly.
When a user runs pytest with a mix of valid paths and excessively long option values, all valid paths should still have their conftests loaded.
When the anchor path existence check raises an OSError for any reason, the anchor should be treated as non-existent and processing should continue without interruption.
When all provided arguments fail path resolution (including due to OSError), pytest should behave the same as when no file anchors are found, proceeding with the default conftest discovery.

task_2.title: Add Python 3.12 compatibility support
task_2.description: pytest 7.3.1 fails to run on Python 3.12 because it relies on deprecated AST node classes (ast.Str, ast.Num, ast.NameConstant) that were removed in Python 3.12, and uses faulthandler file-object patterns that are incompatible with Python 3.12 changes. This update introduces version-conditional aliases for the removed AST classes, fixes the faulthandler integration to use raw file descriptors, updates the mark expression parser for AST compatibility, and corrects file-creation mode in the legacy path utility.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement:
Ensure that pytest runs correctly on Python 3.12 without raising errors due to removed AST node types or incompatible faulthandler file handling. Specifically:
- Ensure the assertion rewriter does not reference ast.Str, ast.Num, or ast.NameConstant directly, as these classes are removed in Python 3.12.
- Ensure the faulthandler integration works correctly on Python 3.12 by using raw file descriptors instead of wrapping them in file objects.
- Ensure the mark expression parser does not reference ast.NameConstant directly.
- Ensure the legacy LocalPath.ensure() method creates files using binary mode to avoid encoding-related issues on Python 3.12.

expectation.grounded: The assertion rewriting module (AssertionRewriter) must use ast.Constant in place of ast.Str, ast.Num, and ast.NameConstant on Python >= 3.8, and fall back to the legacy AST classes on Python < 3.8. The faulthandler plugin must store a duplicated stderr file descriptor as an integer (via os.dup) and pass it directly to faulthandler.enable(file=...) and faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(file=...), closing it with os.close() during unconfiguration. The mark expression parser must use ast.Constant in place of ast.NameConstant on Python >= 3.8. The docstring detection in assertion rewriting must read the docstring value via the .value attribute on ast.Constant nodes (Python >= 3.8) rather than the .s attribute. The variables_overwrite dictionary in boolean operation and comparison rewriting must store the NamedExpr AST node rather than a plain variable name string.
expectation.conceptual: pytest's assertion rewriting, faulthandler integration, mark expression parsing, and legacy path utilities must all function correctly on Python 3.12 without referencing any AST classes or APIs that were removed in that version. Faulthandler must remain operational throughout the test session, including per-test timeout tracebacks. Assertion rewriting must correctly generate rewritten assertion code, including docstring-based rewrite disabling, named expression handling in boolean/comparison operations, and explanation formatting.

constraints.grounded: All changes must maintain backward compatibility with Python 3.7 by retaining fallback usage of ast.Str, ast.Num, and ast.NameConstant on Python < 3.8. The faulthandler must still correctly duplicate stderr, enable fault handling at configure time, dump tracebacks on test timeouts, and properly clean up the file descriptor at unconfigure time. Assertion rewriting behavior must remain identical on all supported Python versions — rewritten assertions must produce the same error messages and explanation formatting. The REWRITE_DISABLED docstring detection must continue to work for both Python < 3.8 and >= 3.8 AST representations.
constraints.conceptual: Backward compatibility with all previously supported Python versions must be preserved. No existing test behavior, assertion output, faulthandler functionality, mark expression evaluation, or file-creation behavior may regress. The changes must be transparent to end users — the same test suites must produce the same results regardless of the Python version within the supported range.

behavior: On Python >= 3.8, the assertion rewriter uses ast.Constant instead of the removed ast.Str, ast.Num, and ast.NameConstant when constructing rewritten AST nodes.
On Python < 3.8, the assertion rewriter continues to use ast.Str, ast.Num, and ast.NameConstant.
Docstring values in assertion-rewritten modules are read via the .value attribute of ast.Constant on Python >= 3.8, and via the .s attribute of ast.Str on older versions.
The faulthandler plugin stores a raw integer file descriptor (from os.dup) instead of a TextIO wrapper, and passes this fd directly to faulthandler.enable() and faulthandler.dump_traceback_later().
The faulthandler plugin cleans up the duplicated file descriptor using os.close() instead of calling .close() on a file object.
The mark expression parser uses ast.Constant(False) instead of ast.NameConstant(False) for empty expressions on Python >= 3.8.
The legacy LocalPath.ensure(file=1) creates files in binary write mode ('wb') instead of text write mode ('w').

In boolean and comparison assertion rewriting, the variables_overwrite dictionary stores the NamedExpr AST node itself rather than a string variable name, enabling correct handling of walrus operator expressions.
acceptance_criteria: When running pytest on Python 3.12, the assertion rewriter must not raise AttributeError for ast.Str, ast.Num, or ast.NameConstant.
When running pytest on Python 3.12, assertion failure messages must display the same formatted explanations as on Python 3.11 and earlier.
When a test module contains a 'PYTEST_DONT_REWRITE' docstring, the assertion rewriter must correctly detect and honor it on Python 3.12.
When the faulthandler timeout is configured and a test exceeds the timeout on Python 3.12, a traceback must be dumped to stderr.
When pytest is unconfigured, the duplicated stderr file descriptor must be properly closed without raising errors.
When evaluating an empty mark expression on Python 3.12, it should return False without raising an AttributeError for ast.NameConstant.
When using LocalPath.ensure(file=1) on Python 3.12, the file must be created successfully without encoding-related errors.
When running pytest on Python 3.7 through 3.11, all assertion rewriting, faulthandler, mark expression, and path behaviors must remain unchanged.
When assertions use named expressions (walrus operator) in boolean or comparison contexts, the rewritten assertions must correctly preserve the named expression nodes for proper evaluation.

task_5.title: Fix walrus operator variable access in assertion rewriting
task_5.description: Fixed a regression in pytest 7.3.x where a variable assigned via the walrus operator (:=) inside an assert statement could not be referenced later in the same expression, such as in a subsequent function call argument. The assertion rewriter now correctly propagates walrus-assigned variables so they resolve properly when reused within the same assert, eliminating the spurious UnboundLocalError.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that variables assigned using the walrus operator (:=) within an assert statement can be referenced in subsequent parts of the same assertion expression, including as positional or keyword arguments to function calls. Previously, pytest 7.3.x raised an UnboundLocalError when a walrus-assigned variable was reused in a function call within the same assert, representing a regression from 7.2.x behavior.

expectation.grounded: When the AssertionRewriter encounters a NamedExpr (walrus operator) in an assert statement, the variables_overwrite mapping must store the original NamedExpr AST node rather than just a renamed variable identifier. During visit of Call nodes, both positional arguments (ast.Name in call.args) and keyword arguments (ast.Name in keyword.value) must be checked against variables_overwrite and substituted with the stored NamedExpr node when matched. Similarly, in comparison visit logic, references to overwritten variables in comp.left must be replaced with the full NamedExpr node, and newly encountered NamedExpr nodes in comp.left must be registered into variables_overwrite. This ensures the rewritten AST correctly binds walrus-assigned variables wherever they are subsequently referenced.
expectation.conceptual: When a walrus operator assigns a variable inside an assert statement, that variable must be accessible and correctly resolved anywhere else it appears in the same assertion expression. This includes use as a function argument, keyword argument, or operand in comparisons. The assertion rewriting mechanism must preserve the binding semantics of the walrus operator so that the rewritten code behaves identically to the original source.

constraints.grounded: The fix must not break existing assertion rewriting behavior for expressions without walrus operators. The variables_overwrite mechanism must continue to handle chained comparisons and boolean operations correctly. When a walrus-assigned variable is referenced in a function call within the same assert, the rewriter must not produce an UnboundLocalError or any other name resolution error. The substitution must apply to both positional and keyword arguments of function calls uniformly.
constraints.conceptual: Existing assertion introspection and rewriting behavior must remain unaffected for all assert expressions that do not use the walrus operator. The fix must not alter the semantics or output of assertion failure messages. All valid Python expressions using the walrus operator within assert statements that worked in pytest 7.2.x must continue to work correctly.

behavior: When the assertion rewriter encounters a walrus operator (:=) in an assert expression, it stores the full named expression AST node in its variable tracking map instead of only a renamed identifier string.

When rewriting function call arguments in an assert expression, the rewriter checks each positional and keyword argument against tracked walrus-assigned variables and substitutes the original named expression node when a match is found.

When rewriting comparison operands, if the left operand references a previously walrus-assigned variable, the rewriter substitutes the full named expression node. If the left operand itself is a new walrus expression, it is registered for subsequent reference resolution.
The UnboundLocalError that previously occurred when a walrus-assigned variable was reused as a function argument within the same assert statement no longer occurs.
acceptance_criteria: When an assert statement uses a walrus operator to assign a variable and then passes that variable as a positional argument to a function call in the same expression (e.g., assert (x := 'foo') in json.dumps(x)), the test should pass without raising UnboundLocalError.

When an assert statement uses a walrus operator to assign a variable and then passes that variable as a keyword argument to a function call in the same expression, the test should pass without raising UnboundLocalError.
When an assert statement uses a walrus operator in a comparison and the assigned variable is referenced in a subsequent operand or function call, the variable should resolve correctly.
Assertion failure messages for expressions containing walrus operators should display meaningful introspection output, consistent with standard assertion rewriting behavior.
All existing assert expressions that do not use walrus operators must continue to work identically, with no change to pass/fail behavior or failure message output.

task_6.title: Fix --last-failed file-skipping for files inside packages
task_6.description: The --last-failed (--lf) flag has an optimization that skips collecting entire files (Modules) when they contain no previously failed tests, reporting them as 'skipped N files' in the collection summary. This optimization only worked for test files located directly at the top level of the test session, but did not apply to test files inside packages (directories containing __init__.py files). The fix extends the file-skipping optimization to also apply when collecting items within packages, so that test files inside packages are correctly skipped when they contain no previously failed tests.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that when using --last-failed (--lf), the file-skipping optimization correctly skips test files inside packages (directories with __init__.py) that contain no previously failed tests, rather than only skipping top-level test files. Previously, test files within packages were still fully collected even when none of their tests had previously failed, defeating the purpose of the optimization and producing incorrect '(skipped N files)' counts.

expectation.grounded: When the LFPluginCollWrapper.pytest_make_collect_report hook processes a collector, it should apply the file-skipping logic for both Session and Package collector types. This means that when --last-failed is active and a Module inside a Package contains no previously failed tests, that Module should be excluded from collection results. The collection summary should accurately report the number of skipped files, including those inside packages.
expectation.conceptual: When running pytest with --last-failed, the file-skipping optimization should work uniformly for all test files regardless of whether they are at the top level or nested inside packages. Test files with no previously failed tests should be skipped during collection, and the summary line should accurately reflect the total number of skipped files including those within packaged directories.

constraints.grounded: The file-skipping behavior for top-level Modules directly under Session must remain unchanged. Only Modules that contain no previously failed tests should be skipped; Modules containing at least one previously failed test must still be collected normally. The fix must not alter collection behavior when --last-failed is not active.
constraints.conceptual: Existing behavior for top-level test files must not regress. The optimization must only skip files that genuinely contain no failed tests. Normal collection behavior without --last-failed must be unaffected.

behavior: When --last-failed is active and a test file inside a package contains no previously failed tests, that file is now skipped during collection instead of being fully collected.
The '(skipped N files)' count in the collection summary now includes files inside packages that were skipped, producing an accurate total.
The file-skipping optimization now operates at both the Session level and the Package level when filtering collection results.
Test files inside packages that do contain previously failed tests continue to be collected and run normally.
acceptance_criteria: When running pytest --last-failed with a previously failed test in a top-level file and a passing-only file inside a package, the packaged file should be reported as skipped in the collection summary.
When running pytest --last-failed, the '(skipped N files)' count should include files inside packages that have no previously failed tests.
When a test file inside a package contains a previously failed test, it should still be collected and run when using --last-failed.
When running pytest without --last-failed, all test files including those inside packages should be collected normally with no behavioral change.
When running pytest --last-failed with multiple packages, files without failures in each package should all be skipped and reflected in the summary count.
